It became the center of his publishing activity, where periodicals first printed his German extracts from the Sentimental Journey. In 1775, it also issued several editions of the Yorick-Eliza letters and related collections, probably translated by Bode and favorably reviewed.

l: London, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: CHAPTER II STERNE IN GERMANY BEFORE THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY It is no exaggeration to assert that the works of Yorick obtained and still retain a relatively more substantial position of serious consideration and recognized merit in France and Germany than in the countries where Sterne’s own tongue is spoken.] London was the center of Sterne’s immediate English triumph after the first two volumes of Tristram Shandy became available there in January 1760. When Sterne arrived in March, aristocratic, ecclesiastical, and literary society received him enthusiastically, and he became one of the most talked-about figures in the city.

l: British supremacy in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: characterizes the sixties [period of Sterne’s literary activity] CHAPTER II STERNE IN GERMANY BEFORE THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY It is no exaggeration to assert that the works of Yorick obtained and still retain a relatively more substantial position of serious consideration and recognized merit in France and Germany than in the countries where Sterne’s own tongue is spoken.] British supremacy in Germany was at its height during the 1760s, when German readers and writers actively engaged with British authors. This cultural situation made the introduction of Sterne into Germany highly probable, despite the delay in his actual recognition.

l: Sterne’s fame in England, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Sterne’s fame in England became immediate after the first two volumes of Tristram Shandy appeared in 1760, bringing rapid renown and a major personal and literary triumph. English enthusiasm later declined into criticism or forgetfulness, before German fame reached its fullest strength and Sterne-worship followed.

l: Zückert’s translation publication history, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Zückert’s translation publication history began with parts I–VI in 1763, expanded with parts VII–VIII in 1765, and added a ninth part in 1767 translated from a spurious English original. A revised, advertised “nach einer neuen Uebersetzung” edition followed in 1769–1772 but retained serious errors and the spurious ninth volume. In 1773 or 1774, Lange reissued it under a title invoking Wieland’s advice, which Wieland denied.

l: Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen is a periodical that first mentioned Sterne on November 15, 1764, reviewing Yorick’s Sermons; by 1767 it explained Yorick, while 1770 sermon reviews referred familiarly to Shandy and The Sentimental Journey.

l: Neue Bibliothek der schönen Wissenschaften, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Neue Bibliothek der schönen Wissenschaften, a periodical, first mentioned Laurence Sterne in its last 1766 number in an article on humor. In 1767 it announced the ninth volume of Tristram Shandy as exceptionally strange wit and humor, while treating Sterne’s German importance condescendingly.

l: Swiss translation of Yorick’s Sermons, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: A Swiss translation of Yorick’s Sermons began publication in 1766, reordered the sermons, and aimed to interest readers in religious discourse; its preface omitted Sterne and Tristram Shandy while addressing cultured readers apart from instruction.

l: German literary world, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: The German literary world initially recognized Sterne and Yorick only limitedly and belatedly, treating Tristram Shandy as a fitful English taste. Educated literati including Herder, Hamann, Riedel, and Wieland selectively read, admired, translated, and discussed it; after The Sentimental Journey, Sterne’s reputation expanded greatly beyond these circles.

l: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing is presented through his sustained admiration for Laurence Sterne and his engagement with Sterne’s writing and reception in Germany. Although the date of his first reading of Tristram Shandy is uncertain, he admired Sterne with remarkable devotion, appreciated him unequivocally, and was later counted among clear-minded critics who recognized Sterne’s importance. After The Sentimental Journey appeared in 1768, Lessing reportedly wished to surrender part of his own life to extend Sterne’s literary activity. He read Bode’s translation in full, approved both the work selected and its translation, and helped shape the rendering of “sentimental” as “empfindsam,” though he is not proven to have proposed the translation. His Sternean engagement also appears in references to Yorick and “Steckenpferd” in letters to Mendelssohn, and in a sermon composed in Yorick’s manner as a trick involving Alberti and Goeze. Lessing owned Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy and marked passages later cited as evidence of Sterne’s borrowings, yet remained silent about those borrowings, apparently judging them unworthy of mention. No later abandonment of his appreciation is recorded.

l: Nicolai, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Nicolai writes a Berlinische Monatsschrift résumé of Ferriar’s findings on Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings. He nonetheless defends Sterne as refined, ingenious, humorous, sensitive, and inventive, arguing that creative additions and distinctive qualities sustain his reputation. From mentioning Yorick early in Sterne’s travel book, he frames source investigation as explanation rather than depreciation.

l: Die Witzlinge, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Die Witzlinge derives directly from Bury Fair, not Tristram Shandy; although once thought to model characters on Sterne’s Trim and Eugenius, the interpretation is rejected, and Lessing’s Trim differs from Corporal Trim.

l: Minna von Barnhelm, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: contains Just [a faithful servant character] Minna von Barnhelm contains passages involving Just, his fidelity, and his exchanges with an innkeeper that have been compared with Sternean scenes. The unit states that a direct connection with The Sentimental Journey is impossible for the relevant episode because the drama appeared nearly a year before that work.

l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Yorick is a clergyman, comic figure, fictional traveler, and literary persona associated with Laurence Sterne. He appears in Tristram Shandy and, as narrator of episodes including the dead ass and Starling in The Sentimental Journey, became the figure through whom German readers chiefly interpreted Sterne’s sentimental qualities. Early German reviews identified him as a clergyman and linked his name on sermons to Sterne; later readers connected him with excellent sermons and sentimental feeling. After The Sentimental Journey reached Germany, German literary and emotional conditions remade Yorick into a delicate, benevolent, morally restrained champion of the oppressed: a model of gentleness, sympathy toward people and animals, and resistance to self-seeking, impropriety, and arbitrary power. The records stress that this was a selective, sometimes superficial conception, reinforced by the Yorick-Eliza letters, translations, and spurious works rather than by a full reading of Sterne’s controlled suggestiveness. This German Yorick became a preceptor in conduct and a powerful literary model. His treatment of Franciscan Lorenzo inspired practical sentimental adherence; his sympathy for animals, whimsical humor, mock-scientific classification of travelers, “hobby-horse” language, blank pages, and other formal vagaries entered discussion, correspondence, and later eccentric writing. He helped establish sentimental ground later associated with The Sorrows of Young Werther and was described as a liberating, beautiful spirit. German writers produced translations, continuations, journeys in Yorick’s manner, and works attributed to his supposed son. Imitators followed his footprints through adapted encounters, humane reflections, sentimental poses, and scenes modeled on Lorenzo, the Monk, and other episodes. Yorick accordingly became both the central emblem of German sentimentalism and a target for satire. Critics objected to followers’ exaggerated sympathy and emotional display while often distinguishing Yorick himself from their excesses; Timme especially used would-be Yoricks to expose sentimental imitation.

l: Uncle Toby, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_related_to Corporal Trim [as master and faithful servant with cordial comradeship] Uncle Toby appears in the account of Lessing’s Yorick’s sermon for Alberti, where he and Trim encounter a wounded French veteran. His compassionate observations provide the structure for Trim’s repeated gifts and the veteran’s recognition as a man, soldier, and unfortunate family man.

l: Corporal Trim, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_a faithful servant [old-fashioned and unquestioningly devoted] Corporal Trim is compared with Lessing’s Just as a faithful servant, though the two characters’ relationships with their masters are not identical. In the reconstructed passage from the Yorick sermon for Alberti, Trim repeatedly gives money to a wounded French veteran and says 'French Dog!' while gradually revealing sympathy.

l: Eugenius, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: that] Eugenius was responsible for the continuation of Yorick’s Journey that Bode translated. Bode omitted, altered, or replaced numerous sections of Eugenius’s narrative, particularly passages considered indecent.

l: Tellheim, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Tellheim in Minna von Barnhelm is not presented as resembling Uncle Toby. His recognition of Just’s unusual fidelity helps explain the significance of the master-servant relationship, but the unit does not establish a direct Sternean model for Tellheim.

l: Just, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_a faithful servant [old-fashioned and unquestioningly devoted] Just is a faithful servant in Minna von Barnhelm whose exchanges with the innkeeper and account of his dog have been compared with Sternean motifs. The unit finds no demonstrated direct borrowing, though it allows that Just may have helped shape Lessing’s later conception of Corporal Trim in the lost sermon.

s: CHAPTER III THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY On February 27, 1768, the Sentimental Journey was published in London,[1] less than three weeks before the author’s death, and the book was at once transplanted to German soil, beginning there immediately its career of commanding influence and wide-spread popularity.] Ebert assisted Bode with the translation of the Sentimental Journey. Bode acknowledged Ebert’s contribution in the preface to the second edition, although Ebert’s role had previously been overlooked in favor of Gotthold Ephraim Lessing’s.

l: Yorick’s sermon for Alberti, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Yorick’s sermon for Alberti is a work written by Gotthold Ephraim Lessing as a trick connected with Alberti’s controversy with Goeze. Privately printed in part by Bode, it opens with Uncle Toby and Corporal Trim aiding a wounded French veteran, imitating Yorick’s sympathetic, tolerant, whimsical simplicity.

l: publication and reception of Sterne in Germany before 1768, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_a period of delayed recognition [despite individual German authors’ earlier acquaintance with Sterne] Before 1768, Sterne’s works reached Germany through translations, catalogues, and reviews, but reception was often belated, incomplete, and condescending. Tristram Shandy attracted notice as an unusual work of humor, while Yorick’s Sermons were initially read mainly as sermons rather than as products of the famous author of Shandy.

l: Johann Georg Hamann, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: shares_devotion_to Laurence Sterne [as indicated by a letter to Herder] Hamann participated with Herder and others in using names from Tristram Shandy, including “Tobias Shandy,” and was addressed through references to Yorick and Trim. A letter from Hamann to Herder dated June 10, 1767, indicates that he shared Herder’s devotion to Sterne.

l: Riedel, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Riedel is a writer and discerning reader of Tristram Shandy. Before Sentimental Journey appeared, he closely appreciated the novel, quoted and translated its Dr. Slop and Obadiah passage, used it to discuss humor and human psychology, wrote Theorie der schönen Künste und Wissenschaften and Ueber das Publikum, and reportedly planned to continue Yorick’s Journey.

l: German eighteenth-century readers, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: lack British humor [with rare exceptions] German eighteenth-century readers generally found Tristram Shandy harder to understand and appreciate than the Sentimental Journey. The text suggests that only rare readers possessed the extensive knowledge of British life and the intensive sympathy with British attitudes needed to grasp Shandy’s humor.

l: Wieland’s proposed translation of Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_a translation of Tristram Shandy [a project probably begun soon after Wieland read Shandy] Wieland’s proposed translation arose from his dissatisfaction with the existing German version and may have involved substantial work, although the correspondence does not establish how much he completed. By December 1769, the Jenaische Zeitungen von Gelehrten Sachen reported that he had given up the project, while suggesting that he might instead write essays functioning as a philosophical commentary on the whole book.

l: Sterne’s stay and death in relation to the reaction against his reputation, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Sturz’s stay in England, from May 6, 1768, to January 14, 1769, followed Sterne’s March 18 death. During this initial English reaction against the reputation and obscenities of the Sterne cult, England began reassessing Sterne and developed a more rational view of his writings.

l: British humor, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_a humor of Shandy [essentially British and difficult to transplant] British humor is presented as a major reason why Tristram Shandy failed to gain immediate broad popularity in Germany. The text describes Shandy’s humor as rooted in eccentricity, British life, and highly individual attitudes that could become obscurity or silliness when transplanted into another language and culture.

l: German sentimentalism, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: German sentimentalism was prepared by Brockes’s sentimental view of nature, fostered by Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock’s emotional poetry, and spread by Christian Fürchtegott Gellert’s religious and ethical sentimentalism. The 1768 publication of the Sentimental Journey brought it to German soil, supplying practical sentimental life and releasing pent-up emotion.

l: interest in travel literature, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: was predominant [in the period surrounding the Sentimental Journey’s publication] CHAPTER III THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY On February 27, 1768, the Sentimental Journey was published in London,[1] less than three weeks before the author’s death, and the book was at once transplanted to German soil, beginning there immediately its career of commanding influence and wide-spread popularity.] Interest in travel literature was unusually strong during the period in which the Sentimental Journey appeared. German presses produced numerous accounts of travel, geography, peoples, and customs, helping the book gain immediate recognition despite its differences from ordinary travel narratives.

l: Böttiger, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: attributes Bode’s authorship of the third and fourth volumes of Yorick’s Journey [partly to the review in the Allgemeine deutsche Bibliothek] that] Böttiger stated that Bode obtained the continuation from Alberti and knew it before anyone else in Germany. He attributed the German coloring of the translation to Bode’s liberties and identified Das Hündchen and Die Moral as additions, although the text says Bode made many more.

l: Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Johann Wolfgang Goethe is presented through his lifelong, discerning engagement with Laurence Sterne and Sterne’s German reception. In Strassburg, under Johann Gottfried Herder’s guidance, Goethe first read Sterne. He then carried Sterne into his own literary circle: recommending him to Jung-Stilling, reading from Tristram Shandy, including the story of poor Le Fevre, to the Darmstadt circle, and repeatedly referring to Sterne and Yorick in letters, works, and conversation. He acknowledged an impulse from Yorick in his travel writing and adopted Sterne’s direct appeal to readers, while distinguishing his own travel accounts from A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy by their objectivity. He regarded Sterne as an adversary of pedantry and philistinism, valued Yorick’s liberating humor and intellectual penetration, and described Sterne as encouraging humane knowledge and tolerance. Goethe also recognized risks in Sterne’s delicately handled indecency. His admiration increased over time: he called himself infinitely indebted to Shakespeare, Sterne, and Goldsmith, reread Sterne near life’s end, and remained unequivocally appreciative even when a new century mocked the earlier fashion. Yet he rejected derivative sentimentality. In 1772 he harshly reviewed Schummel’s work as a contrived imitation, a thistle on Yorick’s grave; Der Triumph der Empfindsamkeit likewise satirized the sentimental movement and imitators of Werther, without being directly tied to Sterne. The record also notes his publication of Koran material without identifying its source, accusations of literary plagiarism involving Sterne and the Koran, and possible Koranic influence on Graf von Gleichen in Stella.

l: Mittelstedt, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Mittelstedt, a pastor and initially anonymous translator, produced a competing German rendering of A Sentimental Journey in Braunschweig. Published in editions dated 1769, following the work’s 1768 London publication, the translation was among its early German versions and became involved in a brief controversy with Bode.

l: Hamburgische Adress-Comptoir-Nachrichten, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: CHAPTER III THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY On February 27, 1768, the Sentimental Journey was published in London,[1] less than three weeks before the author’s death, and the book was at once transplanted to German soil, beginning there immediately its career of commanding influence and wide-spread popularity.] The Hamburgische Adress-Comptoir-Nachrichten printed Johann Joachim Christoph Bode’s translation of “Die Bettler” on April 20, 1768. It later published his two-part translation of the “Monk,” transferring the story of Lorenzo and the snuff-box to German readers within a few months of the English publication.

l: Maria of Moulines, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: appears_in Sentimental Journey [as the subject of a sentimental episode] CHAPTER III THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY On February 27, 1768, the Sentimental Journey was published in London,[1] less than three weeks before the author’s death, and the book was at once transplanted to German soil, beginning there immediately its career of commanding influence and wide-spread popularity.] Maria of Moulines appears in the Sentimental Journey as the subject of a deeply sentimental episode. Her sad fate helped draw German readers back to the related passage in Tristram Shandy and contributed to the emotional power of Sterne’s German reception.

l: Lorenzo, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Lorenzo, a Franciscan monk, is honored by Jacobi and his companions as a model of gentleness, contentment, patience, and forgiveness; they esteem him above calendar saints, believe he deserves canonization, and link his memory with the Lorenzodosen.

l: publication of the Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: The publication of the Sentimental Journey was an event in London on February 27, 1768, less than three weeks before Laurence Sterne’s death. It rapidly reached Germany, where competing translations, extensive discussion, wide popularity, and recognition of Sterne as a literary leader followed. The publication connected Sterne with German literary impulses and emotional experiences and renewed German curiosity about the previously incomprehensible Tristram Shandy. Its influence also appeared in Pankraz’s sentimental journey, which repeats Sterne-derived motifs before turning into a practical joke against him as Pankraz slavishly treats his own disasters as parallels to Yorick’s experiences.

l: Bode’s translation of the Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Bode’s translation of the Sentimental Journey was published by Cramer in Hamburg and Bremen, probably in September or October 1768, with its volumes printed at Bode’s own press. Lessing read the whole translation, and Ebert aided it. Its preface declared an early Sterne cult, discussed translating “sentimental,” and sketched Sterne’s life and works; a second edition followed in 1769.

l: Mittelstedt translation, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Mittelstedt translation is a German rendering of the Sentimental Journey. Published in Braunschweig in September or October 1768 under a title referring to Yorick’s travels, it proposed “Gefühlvolle Reisen” among German equivalents for “sentimental,” reached a second edition in 1769, and prompted a journal dispute with Bode.

l: translation of “sentimental” as “empfindsam”, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: was_coined_by Gotthold Ephraim Lessing [for Bode’s translation] CHAPTER III THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY On February 27, 1768, the Sentimental Journey was published in London,[1] less than three weeks before the author’s death, and the book was at once transplanted to German soil, beginning there immediately its career of commanding influence and wide-spread popularity.] The translation of “sentimental” as “empfindsam” was proposed by Gotthold Ephraim Lessing after Bode had first considered “sittlich.” Bode adopted the new word in his published title, and it became an important part of the German presentation of Sterne’s work.

l: the word “sentimental”, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: CHAPTER III THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY On February 27, 1768, the Sentimental Journey was published in London,[1] less than three weeks before the author’s death, and the book was at once transplanted to German soil, beginning there immediately its career of commanding influence and wide-spread popularity.] The word “sentimental” presented German translators with a significant difficulty because it was regarded as new and lacked a direct German equivalent. Bode’s preface states that Gotthold Ephraim Lessing recommended “empfindsam,” while later discussion noted that Laurence Sterne had not actually coined the English word.

l: Lorenzo episode, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,] The Lorenzo episode provides the direct model for Göchhausen’s scene involving the postman, postage money, the author’s capricious behavior, and subsequent self-reproach. It also informs the treatment of poor wandering monks and the recurring importance of the Lorenzodose.

l: the Maria incident, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: influenced German readers [by arousing sentimental enthusiasm] CHAPTER III THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY On February 27, 1768, the Sentimental Journey was published in London,[1] less than three weeks before the author’s death, and the book was at once transplanted to German soil, beginning there immediately its career of commanding influence and wide-spread popularity.] The Maria incident in the Sentimental Journey was especially effective in arousing German emotional enthusiasm. Its appeal encouraged readers to seek out the corresponding passage in Tristram Shandy, where the episode had been obscured by the surrounding Shandean manner.

l: the third and fourth volumes of Yorick’s Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: The third and fourth volumes of Yorick’s Journey were published in England in spring 1769, where they received unfavorable criticism and little popularity; Bode’s extensively divergent translation, especially of the fourth volume, brought them greater favor in Germany.

l: Allgemeine deutsche Bibliothek, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: reviews the translation of the third and fourth volumes [while suggesting only the possibility of German authorship] that] The Allgemeine deutsche Bibliothek reviewed Bode’s translation and helped spread suspicion of German authorship, although its reviewer only suggested that possibility. The review inferred this from German customs, motifs, word-play, and contemporary literary allusions that seemed inconsistent with a literal translation.

l: Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: influences Karl Blumenberg, eine tragisch-komische Geschichte [through its vagaries] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,] The work is referred to through its abbreviated title, Shandy, as a source that some authors claimed not to have read before composing their own books. The Leben und Schicksale des Martin Dickius is said to imitate Sterne in places, and its digression on noses is treated as suspicious.

l: Das Hündchen, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Das Hündchen is a brief episode added by Bode to his translation of the third and fourth volumes of Yorick’s Journey, replacing the Rue Tireboudin episode. A boy grieves for his dead dog and rejects promises of others; critics praised its pathos, though it differs from Sterne’s sentiment and whimsy.

l: Das Mündel, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Das Mündel is a substantial fiction addition by Bode, a masculine companion-piece linked to Maria of Moulines, following gifted miller’s son Jacques from obstructed love through confinement and bereavement to mental collapse.

l: Walter Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Walter Shandy is a visitor to M’lle Gillet in Bode’s alteration of Vendredi-Saint and an advocate of the favorite contention that great events depend fortuitously on insignificant details. He is represented through this theory and the importance of Christian names; these ideas were adopted in German fiction, echoed in Tobias Knaut, and later cited in Der Roman meines Lebens.

l: Jacobi, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Johann Georg Jacobi is a German author, Fritz Jacobi’s brother, and one of the best-known, typical German disciples and imitators of Laurence Sterne. After reading Sterne’s account of Franciscan Lorenzo with his brother and several ladies, he introduced the Lorenzodosen as a practical sentimental custom. He explained it in an open letter to Gleim published in the Hamburgischer Correspondent, promoted it among friends, and later observed that merchants had made it a commercial speculation; the conceit also linked him to Yorick. In Gleim’s circle he was called Uncle Toby. His Winterreise and Sommerreise, the latter published in late September 1769, imitate Sterne’s sentimental travel writing, with Winterreise also externally influenced by Chapelle. Jacobi exaggerates Yorick’s sentimentalism but largely avoids Sterne’s whimsical side, adding exuberant fancy, mythological figures, serious advocacy of immortality, sympathy for animals, and humane religious characters. His youth works and indebtedness to Sterne became subjects of study. His success and Winterreise helped influence Johann Christian Bock’s Die Tagereise, especially its verse within prose travel narrative, and he remained associated with the sentimental fashion and Lorenzodosen.

l: the translation of the third and fourth volumes, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: A translation of the third and fourth volumes, it begins by preserving some original material, then adds extensive new content, including German literary coloring and over fifty pages of additions, without explanatory comment.

l: Bode’s additions and alterations, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Bode’s additions and alterations are a divergence from the original whose exact extent is unstated. They include substantial fiction, added episodes and digressions, explanations, and other material, occupying about thirty-three of 142 first-volume pages and over fifty second-volume pages. They also alter or omit passages to reduce indecency and shift M’lle Laborde’s visit from Yorick to Walter Shandy.

l: German literary coloring, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_added_by Bode [through German allusions and German word-plays] that] German literary coloring appears through German customs, allusions, word-play, and references to contemporary literary figures and works. Böttiger recognized this coloring but supplied an unsupported explanation that Bode felt free to depart from Sterne because he was no longer dealing with him.

l: Sterne in Germany after the Publication of the Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: CHAPTER IV STERNE IN GERMANY AFTER THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY The publication of the Sentimental Journey, as implied in the previous chapter, brought Sterne into vital connection with literary impulses and emotional experiences in Germany, and his position as a leader was at once recognized.] This unit describes the expansion of Sterne’s German reputation after the Sentimental Journey, including journal reviews, translations, Bode’s prominence, the idealization of Yorick, and the renewed interest in Tristram Shandy and Sterne’s letters.

l: German literary culture, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: CHAPTER IV STERNE IN GERMANY AFTER THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY The publication of the Sentimental Journey, as implied in the previous chapter, brought Sterne into vital connection with literary impulses and emotional experiences in Germany, and his position as a leader was at once recognized.] German literary culture responded enthusiastically to Sterne, with learned journals reviewing his works and readers subscribing to Bode’s translations. Writers and critics frequently praised Bode as an exceptional translator and treated Sterne’s works as tests of emotional and intellectual responsiveness.

l: Lydia Sterne de Medalle, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: edited publication of Sterne’s letters [in three volumes] CHAPTER IV STERNE IN GERMANY AFTER THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY The publication of the Sentimental Journey, as implied in the previous chapter, brought Sterne into vital connection with literary impulses and emotional experiences in Germany, and his position as a leader was at once recognized.] Lydia Sterne de Medalle edited and published a three-volume collection of Sterne’s letters in 1775. She also explained that the publication fulfilled her mother’s wishes concerning Sterne’s correspondence and added a fragment in the manner of Rabelais and an autobiographical piece written for her.

l: Mrs. Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: possessed Sterne’s correspondence [after her husband’s death] CHAPTER IV STERNE IN GERMANY AFTER THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY The publication of the Sentimental Journey, as implied in the previous chapter, brought Sterne into vital connection with literary impulses and emotional experiences in Germany, and his position as a leader was at once recognized.] Mrs. Sterne initially wished that her husband’s correspondence would not be published unless other letters bearing his name appeared. The text presents her restraint in withholding the letters during years of financial difficulty as evidence of delicate feeling.

l: David Garrick, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: David Garrick, an intimate friend of Laurence Sterne, told Helfreich Peter Sturz that Sterne was morally and sexually loose, recounting obscenities that drove ladies away and damaged Sterne’s London reputation.

l: “Letters from Yorick to Eliza”, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Letters from Yorick to Eliza is a brief, anonymously published collection of letters, issued early in 1775 and presented as faithfully copied with Eliza’s permission. The text did not question its authenticity. Its English edition was reviewed in German journals and translated in Hamburg in 1775; reviewers emphasized its tenderness, moral character, and authenticity, and particularly praised Bode’s translation.

l: Eliza, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: wrote journal [on the vessel and at Madeira] Eliza was the subject of a widely translated correspondence with Yorick. German publications presented letters from Eliza and letters to her, while reviewers debated the authenticity and moral character of the relationship.

l: the Sentimental Journey translations, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: CHAPTER IV STERNE IN GERMANY AFTER THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY The publication of the Sentimental Journey, as implied in the previous chapter, brought Sterne into vital connection with literary impulses and emotional experiences in Germany, and his position as a leader was at once recognized.] The Sentimental Journey translations by Bode and Mittelstedt were repeatedly reviewed and compared in German journals. Bode’s version was generally preferred, although Mittelstedt’s rendering was judged more correct in some passages.

l: Bode’s translation of Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Bode’s translation of Tristram Shandy was completed in summer 1774. Praised as a masterly achievement for approximating Sterne’s style, it generally preserved the original’s spirit with fidelity. Its subscription list recorded upwards of 650 subscribers. It later served as the basis for Benzler’s revised edition and for another revision issued in 1831.

l: publication of Sterne’s letters, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: The publication of Sterne’s letters began in 1775 through Letters from Yorick to Eliza, Sterne’s Letters to His Friends, and Lydia Sterne de Medalle’s three-volume collection. That collection included Fragment in the manner of Rabelais and a June dedication to Garrick. Some letters’ authenticity remained uncertain, though others were accepted or standardly edited.

l: the German reading of Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: CHAPTER IV STERNE IN GERMANY AFTER THE PUBLICATION OF THE SENTIMENTAL JOURNEY The publication of the Sentimental Journey, as implied in the previous chapter, brought Sterne into vital connection with literary impulses and emotional experiences in Germany, and his position as a leader was at once recognized.] The German reading of Yorick emphasized his delicacy, sentiment, moral generosity, and ability to bring potentially indecorous situations to decorous conclusions. The text characterizes this interpretation as an idealization produced by reading Sterne at a distance and failing to recognize the complexities of the author’s irony.

l: Yorick-Eliza correspondence, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_a correspondence [associated with Sterne] The Yorick-Eliza correspondence was especially successful with German readers. Reviewers generally regarded the relationship as extraordinarily tender but Platonic, although some questioned whether the letters were original or genuine.

l: “Sermons to Asses”, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: A work mistakenly associated with Sterne in German publications and translations, actually written by Rev. James Murray, attacking the established church, taxation, and coercive power.

l: Koran, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: The Koran is a spurious, purportedly posthumous work attributed to Laurence Sterne, though probably written by Richard Griffith. English critics considered it manifestly spurious, while Germany gave it greater recognition: it was translated in 1771 and 1778, reprinted in Vienna by Sammer in 1795, and accepted or praised by reviewers despite doubts. Not clearly sundered from the original in Germany, it contains Graf von Gleichen and supplied twenty sayings and reflections for the appendix to Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years.

l: Platonic affection, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: describes Yorick-Eliza correspondence [as an interpretation of the relationship] Platonic affection was the interpretation German reviewers applied to the tenderness of the Yorick-Eliza relationship. They argued that virtue and rectitude were preserved despite the correspondence’s emotional warmth.

l: authenticity of Sterne’s letters, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: A topic of repeated German debate, especially over the Yorick-Eliza letters: some reviewers accepted them as genuine, others suspected fabricated letters or collections; Frankfurter Gelehrte Anzeigen defended authenticity vigorously.

l: “Sermons to Asses” authorship controversy, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: concerns Sterne [the work was mistakenly associated with him in Germany] The “Sermons to Asses” authorship controversy arose because German translations and criticism attributed the work to Sterne. The unit states that Rev. James Murray was its actual author and suggests that the German attribution resulted from ignorance, imitation, or a one-sided understanding of Sterne.

l: Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Sterne’s extensive, high-handed unacknowledged appropriation was noted in Germany after George Ferriar’s English investigations, yet scarcely harmed admirers’ regard and remained unavoidable in English literary discussions.

l: George Ferriar, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: George Ferriar, an investigator in England, examined Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, citing Burton passages as theft; his findings were favorably presented by Friedrich Nicolai and prompted attacks by Johann Friedrich Böttiger and Lichtenberg.

l: English imitations of Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: English imitations of Sterne, largely echoing the Sentimental Journey, reached Germany through translations, adaptations, and reprints. Often grouped with Yorick production, they included borrowings, continuations, sequels, and Sterne-like fragments, expanding from individual imitations into a broader German reception.

l: Lorenzodosen, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Lorenzodosen are horn snuff-boxes associated with Yorick and Franciscan Lorenzo. Marked “Pater Lorenzo” outside and “Yorick” on the open lid, they commemorate an emotional response to Sterne’s story and express a sentimental creed: gentleness and restraint of anger. Manufactured and sold commercially, they became a fad among teary sentimental enthusiasts, circulating in Germany and beyond. One Lorenzodose, sent by J . . . to the author of M . . . R . . ., repeatedly restores the author’s sentimental focus and prompts reflections on conduct toward the postman. Lichtenberg’s writings make it an object of ridicule.

l: Winterreise, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Winterreise is a sentimental journey narrative by Johann Georg Jacobi, published in Düsseldorf in June 1769. Alternating prose and verse through short, unnumbered chapters, it unfolds as sentimental travel episodes emphasizing fancy, feeling, moral instruction, sympathy for animals, and humane religious encounters.

l: Johann Peter Eckermann, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: edits Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years [by adding Goethe’s miscellaneous notes to the thin final volumes] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.] Johann Peter Eckermann recorded several of Johann Wolfgang Goethe’s statements about Laurence Sterne. Goethe compared Eckermann to a second Shandy, while Eckermann discussed Sterne’s descriptions and ideas in conversation with Goethe.

l: The Sorrows of Young Werther, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: The Sorrows of Young Werther is a work built on sentimentalism, on groundwork Goethe said Yorick helped prepare. Though no direct Sterne influence is demonstrable, it reflects a mental and emotional condition Sterne contributed to. Alongside Siegwart and Sterne, it was a principal target of Timme’s satire amid a sentimental frenzy.

l: Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: contains The Koran [in the appendix “Aus Makariens Archiv”] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.] Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years included appendices containing miscellaneous sayings and reflections, among them material taken from The Koran and comments on Laurence Sterne. The material was added when the publisher found that the final two volumes were too thin, and it was later reprinted among Goethe’s posthumous works.

l: Goethe’s indebtedness to Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.] Goethe’s indebtedness to Sterne is expressed directly in his statement that he was infinitely indebted to Shakespeare, Sterne, and Goldsmith. He also described Sterne’s influence as formative at the chief point of his development and praised Sterne’s irony, broad outlook, gentleness toward opposition, and equanimity.

l: literary plagiarism, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.] The question of literary plagiarism arises from Goethe’s publication of sayings in Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years that were later identified as translations from The Koran, Laurence Sterne’s best-known forgery. Alfred Hédouin located the sources, while Robert Springer incorrectly stated that the material had only appeared after Goethe’s death; the unit establishes that it had been published during Goethe’s lifetime.

l: Strassburg, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.] Strassburg was where Johann Wolfgang Goethe seems first to have read Laurence Sterne’s works under Johann Gottfried Herder’s guidance. Letters from Goethe’s Strassburg period also suggest that Sterne remained highly esteemed by Herder.

l: German literature of the latter part of the eighteenth century and the beginning of the nineteenth, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_different_because_of Laurence Sterne [in relatively subordinate manifestations] It developed secondary manifestations of Laurence Sterne’s influence, including discontinuous narration, unrelated episodes, typographical eccentricity, direct conversation with the reader, and the adoption of Sternean ideas. German writers also used the hobby-horse, Yorick’s traveler classifications, and the theory that insignificant details determine great events.

l: hobby-horse theory, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_received_by Germany [warmly and permanently] It was warmly received in Germany and became a permanent figure, often with reminders of Yorick’s use of the term. The Revelation of St. John in “Sebaldus Nothanker” and Schottenius’s fifty-seven sermons are presented as hobby-horses, while Lessing also used the term.

l: fortuitous dependence of great events upon insignificant details, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_a principle in fiction [for developing events or character] It became a principle for developing events or character in German fiction. The idea is described as unquestionable in Wezel’s “Tobias Knaut” and as being appropriated wholesale in “Die Grosse Begebenheit aus kleinen Ursachen.”

l: Die Grosse Begebenheit aus kleinen Ursachen, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Die Grosse Begebenheit aus kleinen Ursachen is Schummel’s three-volume work: it begins by imitating Sterne’s two novels, embedding Sterne elements in another narrative fabric, grows increasingly contradictory toward that model, and ends with an admission of its faults and few original beauties.

l: Tobias Knaut, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Tobias Knaut is a humorous eighteenth-century novel, probably the best-known German novel to adopt the style of Tristram Shandy. Beginning ab ovo, it unfolds more extensively through episodes and digressions, readerly addresses, blank pages, mock scholarship, fragments, and typographical play. It treats great events as fortuitously dependent on insignificant details, reflects Henry Fielding and Laurence Sterne, satirizes Empfindsamkeit and originality, and includes Original, whose poems are lost documents.

l: Knigge, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Knigge is a writer only remotely connected with Laurence Sterne. Reise nach Braunschweig contains Schottenius and resembles Fielding and Smollett more than Sterne, despite readerly conversation and a possible hobby-horse motif. He also authored Peter Claus and the epistolary love story Der Roman meines Lebens, neither a Sterne imitation.

l: Jacob Minor, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: writes Wahrheit und Lüge auf dem Theater und in der Literatur [in a suggestive article in Euphorion] In an article in Euphorion, he argued that Sterne helped sharpen observation of self-deception in small matters and of the human soul’s deceiving impulses. He held that Sterne inspired Wieland and Goethe to combat false ideals and life-lies, and that Tieck was schooled in Sterne for portraying conscious or unconscious life-lies.

l: Schummel, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Schummel, born in May 1748, was a German author, writer, and pedagogue who later attained some eminence. As a young man, after reading Laurence Sterne, he wrote Empfindsame Reisen durch Deutschland as an imitator of Sterne, using quotations from Sterne’s Journey and adopting sentimental relationships, digressions, interruptions, typographical devices, experiments, coined words, and Yorickian borrowings. Its central events were generally independent, but the second volume became especially incoherent; by the third, he largely left Sterne’s manner behind, mixed narratives and dramatic pieces, and condemned weaknesses in his own work. He also wrote the fourth part of Die Gleichheit der menschlichen Herzen, published Uebersetzer-Bibliothek, Fritzen’s Reise nach Dessau, and, about fifteen years later, Reise durch Schlesien. The later travel works were largely free of Sterne-like whim and sentiment, and Reise durch Schlesien contrasts his earlier sentimental extravagance with a more worldly attitude.

l: Empfindsame Reisen durch Deutschland, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Empfindsame Reisen durch Deutschland is Johann Gottlieb Schummel’s three-volume acknowledged imitation of Yorick, published by Zimmermann in Wittenberg and Zerbst from Easter 1771 to spring 1772. A typical, well-known German disciple work, it contributes to sentimentalism as document and example. It draws most constantly on A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy, while adapting ideas, motifs, expression, and method from Tristram Shandy.

l: sentimental journeying, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Sentimental journeying is a widely imitated German literary form associated with Yorick, Jacobi, Bock, Schummel, and later writers. It centers on emotional encounters, sympathy for poor people and animals, self-questioning about trivial acts, and seeking sentimental scenes. Influenced by Sterne, it was adopted by Thümmel with less whimsy; by the late eighteenth century it was satirized and called a forced mixture of names, wit, and weak humor.

l: the second volume, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: The second volume of Schummel’s three-volume work becomes more incoherent and less eventful than the first. It mixes the rescued baker’s wife’s sentimental story with Shandean borrowings, digressions, typographical experiments, mock-scientific passages, whimsy, and anticipated censure, while its changed manner foreshadows the third volume.

l: the third volume, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: This third volume is a collection of distinct, loosely connected parts linked by a conventional introductory thread and bearing little relation to Laurence Sterne beyond its title. It begins with the story of Caroline and Rosenfeld, then includes the hosts’ ballad, a play, and an honest preacher’s journal. It returns to sentimental adventures, vicarious begging for a maimed soldier-beggar and a child-murderess visit marked by a blank page, before ending with extended commentary on Schummel’s own work.

l: the third volume’s concluding self-criticism, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: The third volume’s concluding self-criticism is an unusually candid end-of-book condemnation of Schummel’s three-volume work, admitting imitation of Sterne, incoherent narration, bad taste, indelicacy, failed whimsical mannerisms, and failure to characterize Germans as Sterne characterized English and French people.

l: Goethe’s review of the second volume, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: condemns Schummel [as a childish imitator] Goethe’s review of the second volume characterizes Schummel as someone who has taken Yorick’s weapons but lacks Yorick’s inward feeling. It contrasts Yorick’s spontaneous laughter and tears with Schummel’s self-conscious effort to calculate how he should appear to readers.

l: Sterne’s peculiar genius, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_appreciated_by Schummel [despite Schummel’s inability to follow Yorick fully] Sterne’s peculiar genius is associated with combining humane and pathetic feeling with whimsy, digression, emotional spontaneity, and unconventional form. Schummel recognizes and imitates these features but is repeatedly shown as unable to reproduce their effectiveness.

l: Shandean narration and stylistic devices, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_imitated_by Schummel [through digressions, typography, coinages and mock-scientific procedures] Shandean narration and stylistic devices in the second volume include backward jumps in the narrative, numerous digressions, promised chapters on extraordinary subjects, black page margins, an upside-down line, irregular printing, dashes and exclamation points, mathematical calculations, mock-scientific descriptions, and coined words. The unit generally treats Schummel’s use of these devices as weak, awkward, or witless imitations.

l: Schummel’s self-criticism, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Schummel’s self-criticism judges his ninety-page autobiography a flawed, excessively imitative attempt at Sterne, failing to characterize the German people and relying more on Fielding and Richardson. It moves from admitting ill-conception and incoherence to condemning the second volume as still worse, while preserving praise for the preacher’s speeches and a few passages.

l: Johann Christian Bock, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Johann Christian Bock was a theater-poet with the Ackerman Company in Hamburg in 1772 and an author active around 1770. He published Die Tagereise in 1770, later reissued as Die Geschichte eines empfundenen Tages, and anonymously wrote several Empfindsame Reise volumes for holiday visits. His works adapted sentimental encounters associated with Sterne, directly and through Jacobi. Critics judged Die Tagereise tiresome and unsuccessful, though it included German patriotism, praise of Gellert, and moral and religious observations.

l: Die Tagereise, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Published in 1770 and reissued in 1775 as Die Geschichte eines empfundenen Tages, Die Tagereise is a prose journey interspersed with verse. It draws partly directly from Sterne and indirectly through Jacobi, adapting sentimental-journey episodes and attitudes associated with Yorick. Critics largely judged it an unsuccessful or tiresome imitation, though it has some genuine originality.

l: Göschen, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Göschen wrote Reise von Johann, a late sentimental journey in which a master and servant travel through southern Germany. Its whimsical, buoyant, episodic narrative includes sentimental scenes, found papers, description, information, and suggestiveness. Though compared with Yorick and La Fleur and misclassified as an imitation of von Thümmel, it was discussed by Schiller and Goethe for the Xenien but not used.

l: Reise von Johann, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Reise von Johann is a Yorick-like travel work following Johann and his master through southern Germany. Their journey includes encounters with maids, found papers, a death-bed scene, a village funeral, the whimsical Furth Catechismus, and a disturbing tale from a ragged woman’s papers. It ends without becoming a Xenien subject.

l: Moritz August von Thümmel, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: adopted sentimental travel [in Reise in die mittäglichen Provinzen von Frankreich] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl] Moritz August von Thümmel adopted Sterne’s general idea of sentimental journeying in Reise in die mittäglichen Provinzen von Frankreich, while largely removing Sterne’s capriciousness and whimsicality. He also followed Sterne in bringing sensuous experience close to the border of the sensual.

l: Empfindsame Reise von Oldenburg nach Bremen, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: Empfindsame Reise von Oldenburg nach Bremen, written by Hanoverian army officer H. J. C. Hedemann, satirizes the sentimentalism of earlier travelers rather than offering conventional tearful sympathy. It proceeds through Sterne-like whimsy, self-conscious writing commentary, mock promises, and self-examination, ending with Das Ständchen and its double entendre.

l: H. J. C. Hedemann, Laurence Sterne in Germany
s: is_a Hanoverian army officer [and author] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f] H. J. C. Hedemann, a Hanoverian army officer, wrote Empfindsame Reise von Oldenburg nach Bremen. Although Ebeling emphatically denied that the book was inspired by Sterne, the unit identifies substantial Sterne-like features in its whimsical form and satirical treatment of earlier sentimental travelers. Hedemann’s narrator deliberately parodies sentimental hesitation, self-examination, conventional charity, falling in love, and the need to fill a travel book with anecdotes.
